modules.title: 01. Security fundamentals
modules.description: The concepts every security engineer uses: confidentiality, integrity, availability, threats, risk, threat modelling and practical cryptography.

lessons.title: CIA, threats, risk and threat modelling
objectives: Explain confidentiality, integrity and availability with examples.
Assess risk as likelihood x impact and prioritise controls.
Threat-model a small system with data flow diagrams and STRIDE.

topics.title: Basics
details: CIA: keep data secret, correct and available. Controls are preventive, detective or corrective; defence in depth layers them.

topics.title: Risk
details: Risk = likelihood x impact; accept, mitigate, transfer or avoid. Focus on the most likely, most damaging scenarios first.

topics.title: Threat modelling
details: Draw data flows and trust boundaries, then ask STRIDE questions (spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege).

reading.locator: OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet in full.

assignment.title: Threat-model your API
instructions: Draw a data flow diagram for one of your projects with trust boundaries.
List at least 12 threats using STRIDE, rate each, and propose controls.
Pick the top three and implement or describe the fixes.
deliverables: Diagram, threat table and fixes.
acceptanceCriteria: Each threat names the asset, the attacker and the control.

questions.prompt: What does STRIDE stand for?
questions.answer: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.

questions.prompt: How is risk usually estimated?
questions.answer: Likelihood multiplied by impact.
questions.explanation: Prioritise by risk, not by fear.

reviewPrompts: Explain defence in depth.
Where are trust boundaries in a web app?

requirements: OWASP Threat Dragon (free, desktop or web) or draw.io for the diagram.
Your own project as the system to model.
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: Everything in this lab already runs for ₹0 on your laptop or in a free browser lab.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: None needed.

lessons.title: Cryptography in practice: hashing, encryption, signatures, TLS and PKI
objectives: Choose hashing, symmetric encryption, asymmetric encryption or signatures for a need.
Explain TLS, certificates and certificate authorities.
Use envelope encryption with a managed key service.

topics.title: Primitives
details: Hash (SHA-256) for integrity; AES-GCM for confidentiality with integrity; RSA/ECDSA signatures prove who signed; key exchange creates shared secrets.

topics.title: TLS and PKI
details: Servers present certificates signed by CAs your system trusts; certificates expire and must be rotated automatically.

topics.title: Key management
details: Envelope encryption: data keys encrypt data; a master key in KMS/Key Vault encrypts data keys; access to the master key is logged.

video.locator: First week's lectures (introduction, stream ciphers) for intuition.

reading.locator: OWASP Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet in full; then the Transport Layer Security Cheat Sheet sections on certificates.

assignment.title: Envelope encryption demo
instructions: Encrypt a file with a random AES-GCM data key in Python, then encrypt the data key with a local RSA key (simulating KMS).
Sign the ciphertext and verify; show tampering fails verification.
Inspect a real website's certificate chain and explain each certificate.
deliverables: Code, outputs and certificate notes.
acceptanceCriteria: Tampering is detected.
The chain explanation is correct.

questions.prompt: What does a digital signature prove?
questions.answer: That the holder of the private key signed the data and it was not changed.

questions.prompt: Why use envelope encryption?
questions.answer: Large data uses fast data keys while a protected master key controls and audits access.

reviewPrompts: Hash vs MAC vs signature?
What happens when a certificate expires?

requirements: Python `cryptography` package and `openssl` on your laptop.

Envelope encryption against the emulator's KMS: AWS emulator on your laptop: Floci (`docker run -p 4566:4566 floci/floci`, no account) or LocalStack (free non-commercial account and auth token), both on http://localhost:4566
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: Everything in this lab already runs for ₹0 on your laptop or in a free browser lab.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: None needed.

modules.title: 02. Identity and access management
modules.description: Most cloud breaches come from identity problems. Learn authentication, MFA, OAuth/OIDC, SSO and least-privilege cloud IAM.

lessons.title: Authentication, MFA, sessions, OAuth 2.0, OIDC and SSO
objectives: Compare passwords, MFA factors and phishing-resistant methods (passkeys).
Explain OAuth 2.0, OIDC and SAML-based SSO.
Manage sessions and tokens securely.

topics.title: Authentication
details: MFA blocks most account takeovers; phishing-resistant factors (FIDO2/passkeys) beat SMS codes.

topics.title: Federation
details: SSO lets one identity provider (Entra ID, Okta) log users into many apps via SAML or OIDC; OAuth issues access tokens for APIs.

topics.title: Sessions
details: Short-lived tokens, secure HttpOnly cookies, rotation and server-side revocation.

reading.locator: NIST SP 800-63B-4: sections on authenticator types and assurance levels (read the summary tables and phishing resistance).

assignment.title: SSO lab
instructions: Run Keycloak in Docker; create a realm, users and an OIDC client.
Log into a small app via OIDC with MFA enabled; inspect the ID and access tokens.
Write which claims you trust and why.
deliverables: Setup notes, token screenshots (no secrets) and analysis.
acceptanceCriteria: MFA is required at login.
Token validation steps are listed correctly.

questions.prompt: Most phishing-resistant common factor?
questions.answer: FIDO2 security keys or passkeys.
questions.explanation: They bind to the real site's origin.

questions.prompt: OAuth vs OIDC?
questions.answer: OAuth delegates access to APIs; OIDC adds authentication and an ID token.

reviewPrompts: Explain SSO to a manager.
Why are SMS codes weak?

requirements: Keycloak in Docker (`quay.io/keycloak/keycloak`, `start-dev`) as a free identity provider with OIDC, SAML and MFA (TOTP with any authenticator app).
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: Everything in this lab already runs for ₹0 on your laptop or in a free browser lab. Keycloak teaches the same protocols as Entra ID and Okta.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: Entra ID itself comes in the Azure free account or your employer's tenant; an Azure free account ($200 credit for 30 days with spending protection; you are not charged unless you move to pay-as-you-go) or, better, ask your employer whether you have a Visual Studio subscription with monthly Azure credit and its spending limit left on. Never remove the spending limit; delete the resource group after each session.

lessons.title: Cloud IAM: policies, roles, least privilege and access reviews
objectives: Read and write AWS IAM and Azure RBAC policies.
Explain AWS policy evaluation (explicit deny, allows, boundaries, SCPs).
Find over-privileged identities and reduce them.

topics.title: Policies
details: AWS: JSON statements with Effect, Action, Resource, Condition. Azure: role definitions assigned at a scope (subscription, resource group, resource).

topics.title: Evaluation
details: In AWS an explicit deny always wins; otherwise you need an allow from identity or resource policies, within permission boundaries and SCPs.

topics.title: Least privilege
details: Start from zero, use access analyzer / activity logs to generate minimal policies, prefer roles over users, review access regularly.

reading.locator: AWS IAM 'Policy evaluation logic' page in full, including the flow chart.

assignment.title: Least-privilege refactor
instructions: In your sandbox, create a role with AdministratorAccess used by a small app.
Use CloudTrail/IAM Access Analyzer to generate a minimal policy; replace and test the app still works.
Write an access-review checklist.
deliverables: Before/after policies, test evidence and checklist.
acceptanceCriteria: The app works with the minimal policy and fails for an action outside it.

questions.prompt: What wins in AWS policy evaluation?
questions.answer: An explicit deny.

questions.prompt: Why prefer roles over IAM users with access keys?
questions.answer: Roles give temporary credentials; keys are long-lived and leak.

reviewPrompts: Write a policy allowing read-only access to one bucket.
What is a permission boundary?

requirements: AWS emulator on your laptop: Floci (`docker run -p 4566:4566 floci/floci`, no account) or LocalStack (free non-commercial account and auth token), both on http://localhost:4566
AWS CLI pointed at the emulator: `aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:4566 ...` with dummy keys (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test`, region us-east-1)
Write the minimal policy by hand from the actions your app calls (the emulator logs each request), instead of using IAM Access Analyzer.
Azure RBAC role definitions can be written and reviewed as JSON without a subscription.
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: The emulator runs the same API calls, CLI commands and Terraform as AWS, so the skills transfer. It does not prove real AWS performance, real IAM enforcement in every service, real networking or real billing. Say 'built and tested against an AWS emulator' unless you also ran the optional real-cloud step. IAM Access Analyzer policy generation needs real CloudTrail data.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: Optional real-cloud step: an AWS account on the Free plan (up to $200 credits for 6 months; no charges unless you upgrade to the paid plan). Never click 'upgrade', set a $1 budget alert anyway, and delete everything after the session. On real AWS, test the minimal policy with the IAM policy simulator.

modules.title: 03. AWS security services
modules.description: Secure an AWS account end to end: logging, threat detection, findings management, encryption and network controls.

lessons.title: Logging and detection: CloudTrail, GuardDuty and Security Hub
objectives: Enable organisation-wide CloudTrail and protect the logs.
Enable GuardDuty and understand its findings.
Aggregate findings and run the CIS standard in Security Hub.

topics.title: CloudTrail
details: Records API calls (who did what, when, from where); send to a separate, locked-down bucket with integrity validation.

topics.title: GuardDuty
details: Analyses CloudTrail, VPC flow and DNS logs to flag threats like credential misuse or crypto-mining.

topics.title: Security Hub
details: Collects findings from AWS services and tools; runs standards such as CIS AWS Foundations; automates responses with EventBridge.

reading.locator: AWS Security Hub: 'What is Security Hub', 'Security standards' (CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark) and 'Automations'.

assignment.title: Secure a sandbox account
instructions: Enable CloudTrail (all regions), GuardDuty and Security Hub with the CIS standard in a sandbox account (watch free-trial periods and costs).
Generate GuardDuty sample findings and route a high-severity finding to email via EventBridge.
Fix five Security Hub CIS failures and record the score change; disable services after if cost matters.
deliverables: Screenshots, EventBridge rule and remediation notes.
acceptanceCriteria: Five CIS controls move from failed to passed.

questions.prompt: What does CloudTrail record?
questions.answer: API calls made in the account: who, what, when and from where.

questions.prompt: What does GuardDuty analyse?
questions.answer: CloudTrail, VPC flow logs and DNS logs (and more) for threats.

reviewPrompts: Why store logs in a separate account?
How do you automate a finding response?

requirements: Study the GuardDuty finding types and the sample finding JSON in the GuardDuty docs; write an EventBridge-style rule and a Python handler that routes a high-severity sample finding.
CloudTrail-style practice: download a public sample CloudTrail dataset (for example the flaws.cloud / Splunk BOTS datasets) and query it with DuckDB or jq.
Security Hub's CIS checks: read the CIS AWS Foundations controls and practise with Prowler (free, open source) on your Free plan account later; some Prowler checks will not work against an emulator.
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: GuardDuty and Security Hub are managed AWS services and are not emulated. You learn their findings and automation without them; you have not operated them.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: Optional real-cloud step: an AWS account on the Free plan (up to $200 credits for 6 months; no charges unless you upgrade to the paid plan). Never click 'upgrade', set a $1 budget alert anyway, and delete everything after the session. Check that a service is available on the Free plan before enabling it, and turn it off after the lab.

lessons.title: Data and network protection: KMS, S3, security groups and private access
objectives: Encrypt data with KMS keys and control key use.
Lock down S3 with Block Public Access and bucket policies.
Design network controls: security groups, NACLs, private subnets and VPC endpoints.

topics.title: Encryption
details: Default encryption with KMS keys; key policies decide who can use keys; rotation is automatic for customer managed keys if enabled.

topics.title: S3
details: Account-level Block Public Access, bucket policies that require TLS and deny unencrypted uploads, access logging.

topics.title: Network
details: Security groups are stateful allow-lists on instances; keep databases in private subnets; reach AWS services through VPC endpoints instead of the internet.

reading.locator: Amazon S3 'Blocking public access to your Amazon S3 storage' in full; then the KMS concepts page.

assignment.title: Lock down storage and network
instructions: Create an S3 bucket with KMS encryption, a TLS-only policy and public access blocked; prove anonymous access fails.
Build a VPC with a private subnet and an S3 gateway endpoint; access S3 from a private instance without internet.
Delete everything afterwards.
deliverables: Terraform or CLI scripts and test evidence.
acceptanceCriteria: Anonymous and non-TLS access are denied.
Private instance reaches S3 only via the endpoint.

questions.prompt: Are security groups stateful?
questions.answer: Yes; return traffic is automatically allowed.

questions.prompt: Why use a VPC endpoint for S3?
questions.answer: Traffic stays on the AWS network without internet access.

reviewPrompts: Write a TLS-only bucket policy condition.
Security group vs NACL?

requirements: AWS emulator on your laptop: Floci (`docker run -p 4566:4566 floci/floci`, no account) or LocalStack (free non-commercial account and auth token), both on http://localhost:4566
AWS CLI pointed at the emulator: `aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:4566 ...` with dummy keys (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test`, region us-east-1)

Terraform pointed at the emulator: in the `aws` provider set `endpoints { ... = "http://localhost:4566" }`, `skip_credentials_validation = true`, `skip_requesting_account_id = true`, `s3_use_path_style = true` (or `pip install terraform-local` and run `tflocal` with LocalStack)
Test the TLS-only and deny-unencrypted bucket policies against the emulator and note any condition it does not enforce.
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: The emulator runs the same API calls, CLI commands and Terraform as AWS, so the skills transfer. It does not prove real AWS performance, real IAM enforcement in every service, real networking or real billing. Say 'built and tested against an AWS emulator' unless you also ran the optional real-cloud step.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: Optional real-cloud step: an AWS account on the Free plan (up to $200 credits for 6 months; no charges unless you upgrade to the paid plan). Never click 'upgrade', set a $1 budget alert anyway, and delete everything after the session.

modules.title: 04. Azure security
modules.description: You already hold several Azure certifications. Learn Azure's security controls in depth: Entra ID, RBAC, Defender for Cloud, Key Vault and Sentinel. This also prepares AZ-500.

lessons.title: Entra ID, Azure RBAC, conditional access and privileged identity management
objectives: Manage users, groups, service principals and managed identities.
Assign Azure RBAC at the right scope.
Explain conditional access and just-in-time admin with PIM.

topics.title: Identities
details: Users and groups for people; service principals and managed identities for apps (managed identities avoid secrets entirely).

topics.title: RBAC
details: Assign built-in roles at the smallest scope; custom roles only when needed; review owner/contributor assignments.

topics.title: Policies
details: Conditional access requires MFA or compliant devices based on risk; PIM grants admin roles just in time with approval and expiry.

reading.locator: Microsoft Entra ID fundamentals: 'What is Microsoft Entra ID?', then the linked conditional access and Privileged Identity Management overviews.

assignment.title: Azure identity hardening
instructions: In a free Azure subscription, create a resource group with a managed identity accessing a storage account via RBAC (no keys).
Write the conditional access policy you would require for admins (on paper if your tenant lacks P1/P2 licences).
List all role assignments and remove any unnecessary ones.
deliverables: CLI/portal evidence and policy design.
acceptanceCriteria: Storage access works through managed identity without account keys.

questions.prompt: Why prefer managed identities?
questions.answer: Azure handles credentials, so there are no secrets to store or leak.

questions.prompt: What does PIM provide?
questions.answer: Just-in-time, time-limited, approved elevation to privileged roles.

reviewPrompts: Explain RBAC scopes.
Service principal vs managed identity?

requirements: Keycloak (free) for groups, roles, client credentials and MFA policies, to practise the same ideas as Entra ID.
Microsoft Learn's free AZ-500 modules and documentation for the Entra-specific screens (the old free Learn sandboxes have been discontinued).
Write the conditional access and PIM design on paper; both need Entra ID P1/P2 licences anyway.
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: Without an Azure tenant you design and explain Entra ID controls rather than click through them. Managed identity testing needs Azure.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: Optional real-cloud step: an Azure free account ($200 credit for 30 days with spending protection; you are not charged unless you move to pay-as-you-go) or, better, ask your employer whether you have a Visual Studio subscription with monthly Azure credit and its spending limit left on. Never remove the spending limit; delete the resource group after each session.

lessons.title: Defender for Cloud, Key Vault and Microsoft Sentinel
objectives: Use Defender for Cloud secure score and recommendations.
Store and access secrets with Key Vault using RBAC.
Connect data to Sentinel and write a simple analytics rule.

topics.title: Posture
details: Defender for Cloud assesses resources against benchmarks and gives a secure score; fix the highest-impact recommendations first.

topics.title: Secrets
details: Key Vault stores secrets, keys and certificates; use RBAC and managed identities; enable soft delete and purge protection; access is logged.

topics.title: SIEM
details: Sentinel ingests logs through connectors, runs KQL analytics rules, groups alerts into incidents and automates with playbooks.

reading.locator: Defender for Cloud introduction; then Key Vault overview and Sentinel overview.

assignment.title: Azure detection loop
instructions: Enable the free tier of Defender for Cloud and fix three recommendations.
Move an app secret into Key Vault accessed by managed identity.
In a Sentinel trial workspace, connect Entra sign-in logs and write a KQL rule for repeated failed sign-ins; remove resources after.
deliverables: Evidence for all three and the KQL rule.
acceptanceCriteria: The KQL rule fires on simulated failed sign-ins.

questions.prompt: What is Defender for Cloud's secure score?
questions.answer: A measure of how many security recommendations are implemented.

questions.prompt: Which query language does Sentinel use?
questions.answer: KQL (Kusto Query Language).

reviewPrompts: Key Vault protections you always enable?
Alert vs incident in Sentinel?

requirements: Secrets: HashiCorp Vault in dev mode (`vault server -dev`, free) or the emulator's Secrets Manager, to practise the same secret-store patterns as Key Vault.
SIEM: Wazuh or the Elastic Stack (free) instead of Sentinel; write your detection in KQL on paper and in the free tool's query language.
Posture: Prowler or ScoutSuite (free) instead of Defender for Cloud recommendations.
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: These free tools teach the same jobs (secret storage, SIEM rules, posture findings); the Azure-specific screens need Azure.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: Optional real-cloud step: an Azure free account ($200 credit for 30 days with spending protection; you are not charged unless you move to pay-as-you-go) or, better, ask your employer whether you have a Visual Studio subscription with monthly Azure credit and its spending limit left on. Never remove the spending limit; delete the resource group after each session. Defender's paid plans and Sentinel ingestion can cost money; keep only the free tier and delete the workspace after.

modules.title: 05. Application security
modules.description: Find and fix vulnerabilities in web applications and automate security testing in CI.

lessons.title: Hands-on OWASP Top 10 with Juice Shop and PortSwigger labs
objectives: Exploit and fix injection, broken access control, XSS and SSRF in local labs.
Use an intercepting proxy to inspect and modify requests.
Write vulnerability reports with impact and remediation.

topics.title: Labs
details: OWASP Juice Shop runs locally in Docker; PortSwigger Web Security Academy has free guided labs. Only attack these intentionally vulnerable targets.

topics.title: Tools
details: Burp Suite Community or OWASP ZAP intercept traffic so you can see and change requests.

topics.title: Reporting
details: Title, severity, affected endpoint, steps to reproduce, impact, fix and how to verify the fix.

reading.locator: PortSwigger Web Security Academy 'Getting started', then the learning material for SQL injection and access control.

assignment.title: Ten vulnerabilities
instructions: Run Juice Shop locally and solve ten challenges across at least five OWASP categories.
Complete five PortSwigger apprentice labs.
Write two full vulnerability reports including the code-level fix.
deliverables: Challenge list, lab completions and two reports.
acceptanceCriteria: Reports include reproduction steps and a verified fix.

questions.prompt: What is SSRF?
questions.answer: Tricking a server into making requests to places the attacker chooses, such as internal services.
questions.explanation: Block with allow-lists and network controls.

questions.prompt: Where may you practise exploiting vulnerabilities?
questions.answer: Only on systems you own or are explicitly authorised to test, such as local labs.

reviewPrompts: Explain stored vs reflected XSS.
What makes a good vulnerability report?

requirements: OWASP Juice Shop in Docker (`docker run -p 3000:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop`).
PortSwigger Web Security Academy labs (free account).
Burp Suite Community Edition or OWASP ZAP (both free).
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: Everything in this lab already runs for ₹0 on your laptop or in a free browser lab.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: None needed.

lessons.title: SAST, DAST, SCA and secrets scanning in CI
objectives: Explain SAST, DAST, SCA and secret scanning and what each misses.
Add Semgrep, Trivy and ZAP to a CI pipeline.
Triage findings: true positive, false positive, accepted risk.

topics.title: Tool types
details: SAST reads source code; DAST attacks a running app; SCA checks dependencies for known CVEs; secret scanners find keys in code and history.

topics.title: Pipelines
details: Fast checks on every PR (Semgrep, secrets, SCA), heavier DAST nightly; fail builds only on high-confidence, high-severity findings at first.

topics.title: Triage
details: Every finding gets an owner and a decision; suppressions require a reason and expiry date.

reading.locator: Semgrep docs: 'Getting started' and 'Run Semgrep in CI'; then Trivy docs 'Overview' and the ZAP baseline scan page.

assignment.title: Security CI
instructions: Add Semgrep, gitleaks and Trivy (filesystem) jobs to one of your repositories.
Add a nightly ZAP baseline scan against the app running in CI.
Triage every finding with a recorded decision.
deliverables: Workflow files and a triage table.
acceptanceCriteria: Each finding has a decision and owner.
A planted vulnerable dependency fails the build.

questions.prompt: SAST vs DAST?
questions.answer: SAST analyses source code; DAST tests the running application.

questions.prompt: What does SCA check?
questions.answer: Third-party dependencies for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) and licences.

reviewPrompts: Which scans run on every PR and why?
How do you handle false positives?

requirements: GitHub Actions on a public repository (standard runners are free for public repos)
Semgrep, gitleaks, Trivy and the ZAP baseline action are free.
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: Everything in this lab already runs for ₹0 on your laptop or in a free browser lab.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: None needed.

modules.title: 06. Software supply-chain security
modules.description: Protect how software is built and shipped: SBOMs, vulnerability management, artifact signing, provenance and admission control.

lessons.title: SBOMs, vulnerability management and dependency hygiene
objectives: Generate SBOMs for images and applications.
Prioritise vulnerabilities by severity, exploitability and reachability.
Keep dependencies updated safely with automated pull requests.

topics.title: SBOMs
details: An SBOM lists every component and version in an artifact (SPDX or CycloneDX); store it with the artifact so you can answer 'are we affected?' quickly.

topics.title: Prioritising
details: Not every CVE matters: consider CVSS, known exploitation (CISA KEV), whether the vulnerable code is reachable and whether a fix exists.

topics.title: Hygiene
details: Pin versions with lockfiles, use Dependabot/Renovate, minimal base images, and remove unused dependencies.

reading.locator: Syft README: installation, generating SBOMs from images and directories, and output formats.

assignment.title: SBOM and triage
instructions: Generate SBOMs for two of your images with Syft; scan them with Trivy or Grype.
Triage the top ten findings using severity, KEV status and reachability.
Rebuild on a smaller base image and compare counts.
deliverables: SBOMs, scan results and triage table.
acceptanceCriteria: Triage decisions cite evidence, not just CVSS.

questions.prompt: What is an SBOM?
questions.answer: A list of components and versions inside a software artifact.

questions.prompt: Is every high CVSS finding urgent?
questions.answer: No, exploitability and reachability matter too.

reviewPrompts: SPDX vs CycloneDX?
How do minimal base images help?

requirements: Syft, Grype and Trivy (free) on your laptop or in GitHub Actions.
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: Everything in this lab already runs for ₹0 on your laptop or in a free browser lab.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: None needed.

lessons.title: Signing, provenance (SLSA) and admission control
objectives: Sign container images keylessly with Cosign and verify them.
Explain SLSA levels and build provenance.
Enforce signed images in Kubernetes with an admission controller.

topics.title: Signing
details: Cosign signs images using short-lived certificates tied to your CI identity (Sigstore); verification checks who built the image.

topics.title: Provenance
details: SLSA provenance records how, where and from what source an artifact was built; higher levels make tampering harder.

topics.title: Enforcement
details: Admission controllers (OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno, Sigstore policy-controller) reject unsigned or vulnerable images at deploy time.

reading.locator: Sigstore docs: 'Overview', Cosign 'Signing containers' and 'Verifying signatures'.

assignment.title: Only signed images run
instructions: Sign images in GitHub Actions with Cosign keyless signing and attach the SBOM as an attestation.
In a kind cluster, install an admission controller that requires your signature.
Show an unsigned image is rejected and a signed one runs.
deliverables: Workflow, policy and demo evidence.
acceptanceCriteria: Unsigned images are blocked at admission.

questions.prompt: What does keyless signing with Sigstore use?
questions.answer: Short-lived certificates bound to an identity such as your CI workflow.
questions.explanation: No long-lived signing key to protect.

questions.prompt: Where are unsigned images blocked?
questions.answer: At Kubernetes admission by a policy controller.

reviewPrompts: Explain SLSA provenance.
Why sign in CI rather than on a laptop?

requirements: GitHub Actions on a public repository (standard runners are free for public repos) with Cosign keyless signing (free public Sigstore).
Kubernetes on your laptop: kind (`kind create cluster`), minikube or k3d; give Docker at least 4 GB RAM with Kyverno or Sigstore policy-controller.
Images in ghcr.io (free for public images).
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: Everything in this lab already runs for ₹0 on your laptop or in a free browser lab.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: None needed.

modules.title: 07. Container and Kubernetes security
modules.description: Harden containers and clusters: image hardening, runtime restrictions, RBAC, network policies and pod security standards.

lessons.title: Hardening containers: non-root, read-only, capabilities and runtime detection
objectives: Build minimal images that run as non-root with read-only filesystems.
Drop Linux capabilities and apply seccomp profiles.
Detect suspicious runtime behaviour.

topics.title: Images
details: Distroless or slim bases, no shells or package managers in production images, pinned digests.

topics.title: Runtime limits
details: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, drop ALL capabilities, RuntimeDefault seccomp.

topics.title: Detection
details: Runtime tools (e.g. Falco) alert on shells spawning in containers or unexpected network connections.

reading.locator: Kubernetes 'Pod Security Standards': the Baseline and Restricted profiles in full.

assignment.title: Restricted workload
instructions: Deploy one of your services to kind with the Restricted pod security profile enforced.
Fix every violation (user, capabilities, filesystem, seccomp).
Show a privileged pod is rejected.
deliverables: Manifests and evidence.
acceptanceCriteria: Your service runs under the Restricted profile.

questions.prompt: Why run containers as non-root?
questions.answer: A compromise then has fewer privileges on the node.

questions.prompt: What does readOnlyRootFilesystem prevent?
questions.answer: Writing to the container's filesystem, blocking many persistence tricks.

reviewPrompts: List the Restricted profile requirements.
Why remove shells from images?

requirements: Kubernetes on your laptop: kind (`kind create cluster`), minikube or k3d; give Docker at least 4 GB RAM with Pod Security Admission labels on a namespace.
Falco (free) for runtime detection, if your laptop kernel supports it.
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: Everything in this lab already runs for ₹0 on your laptop or in a free browser lab.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: If Falco will not load on your machine, skip runtime detection and use a Killercoda playground for that step.

lessons.title: Kubernetes RBAC, network policies and secrets
objectives: Write least-privilege Roles and RoleBindings and audit service accounts.
Isolate namespaces with default-deny network policies.
Handle Kubernetes secrets safely (encryption at rest, external secret stores).

topics.title: RBAC
details: Roles grant verbs on resources in a namespace; avoid cluster-admin for workloads; disable automounting service account tokens when not needed.

topics.title: Network policies
details: Pods accept all traffic by default; a default-deny policy plus explicit allows limits lateral movement (needs a CNI that enforces policies).

topics.title: Secrets
details: Secrets are base64, not encrypted, unless etcd encryption is enabled; external stores (Vault, cloud secret managers) via CSI or operators are safer.

reading.locator: Kubernetes 'Using RBAC Authorization' in full; then the 'Network Policies' concept page.

assignment.title: Segment a cluster
instructions: Create two namespaces (frontend, backend) with default-deny policies and one allowed flow.
Give a CI service account rights to deploy in one namespace only; prove other actions fail with `kubectl auth can-i`.
Run kube-bench or a similar CIS check and fix two findings.
deliverables: Manifests, test commands and findings.
acceptanceCriteria: Blocked traffic and denied actions are demonstrated.

questions.prompt: Are Kubernetes Secrets encrypted by default?
questions.answer: No, they are only base64-encoded unless encryption at rest is configured.

questions.prompt: What is the default network behaviour between pods?
questions.answer: All traffic is allowed.

reviewPrompts: Write a default-deny policy.
How do you audit service account permissions?

requirements: Kubernetes on your laptop: kind (`kind create cluster`), minikube or k3d; give Docker at least 4 GB RAM. Recent kind versions (v0.24 and later) enforce NetworkPolicy with the default CNI; on older versions install Calico.
kube-bench (free) for CIS checks.
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: Everything in this lab already runs for ₹0 on your laptop or in a free browser lab.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: If your NetworkPolicy has no effect, upgrade kind or install Calico, or use a Killercoda playground.

modules.title: 08. Detection engineering and SIEM
modules.description: Turn logs into reliable detections: SIEM pipelines, Sigma rules, MITRE ATT&CK mapping and testing with Atomic Red Team.

lessons.title: Security logging and SIEM pipelines
objectives: Choose which logs to collect for endpoints, cloud and applications.
Set up a lab SIEM (Wazuh or Elastic) collecting Sysmon and auditd data.
Normalise and search events.

topics.title: Sources
details: Cloud audit logs, identity provider sign-ins, endpoint telemetry (Sysmon on Windows, auditd on Linux), DNS, proxy and application logs.

topics.title: Pipeline
details: Collect -> parse/normalise -> enrich -> store -> detect -> alert; consistent field names make rules portable.

topics.title: Hygiene
details: Protect logs from tampering, keep retention long enough for investigations, avoid logging secrets.

reading.locator: Wazuh docs: 'Getting started' (components and architecture) and the quickstart installation.

assignment.title: Lab SIEM
instructions: Install Wazuh (or Elastic) in Docker/VMs with one Windows (Sysmon) and one Linux (auditd) agent.
Generate normal activity and search for logons, process creation and file changes.
Document your log sources and retention.
deliverables: Lab setup notes and example searches.
acceptanceCriteria: Events from both endpoints are searchable.

questions.prompt: What does Sysmon add on Windows?
questions.answer: Detailed process, network and file telemetry.

questions.prompt: Why protect logs from tampering?
questions.answer: Attackers try to delete evidence.
questions.explanation: Ship them off the host quickly.

reviewPrompts: List your top five log sources.
Why normalise field names?

requirements: Wazuh via its Docker single-node deployment, a Linux VM with auditd, and a Windows VM with Sysmon if you have one (a Windows 11 Enterprise evaluation ISO is free for 90 days; otherwise use two Linux agents).
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: Everything in this lab already runs for ₹0 on your laptop or in a free browser lab. Wazuh needs about 4-8 GB of RAM.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: On a low-RAM laptop use the Elastic Stack with a single node or just Sysmon/auditd logs searched with jq.

lessons.title: Sigma rules, MITRE ATT&CK and validating detections with Atomic Red Team
objectives: Write Sigma rules and convert them to SIEM queries.
Map detections to ATT&CK techniques and find coverage gaps.
Validate every rule with an Atomic Red Team test in the lab.

topics.title: Sigma
details: YAML rules with logsource, detection selections and conditions; sigma-cli converts them to Splunk, Elastic, Sentinel or Wazuh queries.

topics.title: ATT&CK
details: Tactics (why) and techniques (how) such as T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter; track coverage in ATT&CK Navigator.

topics.title: Validation
details: Run the matching Atomic test, confirm the alert fires, tune false positives against normal activity, keep rules in Git with CI.

reading.locator: Sigma docs: 'Getting started', 'Rules' (logsource, detection, condition) and 'Converting rules' with sigma-cli.

assignment.title: Ten validated detections
instructions: Pick ten ATT&CK techniques relevant to your lab; write a Sigma rule for each.
Run the Atomic Red Team test for each in the isolated lab and record whether it fired.
Tune noisy rules; publish an ATT&CK Navigator layer of your coverage.
deliverables: Rules repo with CI, test log and coverage layer.
acceptanceCriteria: Every rule has a recorded Atomic test result.

questions.prompt: What is Sigma?
questions.answer: A generic, SIEM-independent format for detection rules.
questions.explanation: Converted into each SIEM's query language.

questions.prompt: How do you know a detection works?
questions.answer: Trigger the technique safely (e.g. Atomic test) and confirm the alert.

reviewPrompts: Write a Sigma rule outline for encoded PowerShell.
Tactic vs technique?

requirements: sigma-cli, MITRE ATT&CK Navigator (web, free) and Atomic Red Team, all free; run tests only inside your isolated lab VMs.
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: Everything in this lab already runs for ₹0 on your laptop or in a free browser lab.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: None needed.

modules.title: 09. Incident response
modules.description: Handle security incidents calmly and correctly: preparation, detection, containment, eradication, recovery and lessons learned.

lessons.title: The incident response lifecycle, playbooks and cloud forensics basics
objectives: Follow the NIST incident response lifecycle.
Write playbooks for common cloud incidents (leaked key, compromised VM, public bucket).
Preserve evidence and communicate during an incident.

topics.title: Lifecycle
details: Prepare, detect and analyse, contain, eradicate, recover, learn. Containment first limits damage; do not destroy evidence.

topics.title: Playbooks
details: Leaked access key: disable key, review CloudTrail for its use, rotate, assess impact. Compromised VM: isolate with security group, snapshot disks, investigate.

topics.title: Communication
details: Clear roles (incident commander, scribe, communications), a timeline, and a blameless post-incident review.

reading.locator: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: read the overview of the incident response life cycle and its mapping to CSF 2.0 functions.

assignment.title: Tabletop exercise
instructions: Write three playbooks: leaked access key, compromised VM, public storage bucket.
Run a tabletop for the leaked key in your sandbox: create a key, 'leak' it to a private file, then follow the playbook using CloudTrail.
Write a post-incident review.
deliverables: Playbooks, exercise timeline and review.
acceptanceCriteria: The playbook was executed end to end in the sandbox.

questions.prompt: First goal after confirming an incident?
questions.answer: Containment, to limit damage, while preserving evidence.

questions.prompt: First step for a leaked cloud access key?
questions.answer: Disable or deactivate the key.
questions.explanation: Then investigate its use and rotate.

reviewPrompts: Name the IR roles.
Why snapshot a compromised VM before rebuilding?

requirements: AWS emulator on your laptop: Floci (`docker run -p 4566:4566 floci/floci`, no account) or LocalStack (free non-commercial account and auth token), both on http://localhost:4566
AWS CLI pointed at the emulator: `aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:4566 ...` with dummy keys (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test`, region us-east-1)
Run the leaked-key tabletop on the emulator: create a key, 'use' it, disable it and review the emulator's request log as your 'CloudTrail'.
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: The playbook steps and commands are real; CloudTrail investigation on the emulator is a simplified stand-in.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: Optional real-cloud step: an AWS account on the Free plan (up to $200 credits for 6 months; no charges unless you upgrade to the paid plan). Never click 'upgrade', set a $1 budget alert anyway, and delete everything after the session. Never put a real key anywhere public, even in a lab.

modules.title: 10. Cloud posture management and compliance
modules.description: Continuously check cloud configuration against benchmarks, scan infrastructure as code before deployment, and map controls to compliance frameworks.

lessons.title: CIS benchmarks and building a posture scanner
objectives: Read CIS cloud benchmarks and map controls to API checks.
Build a small scanner with boto3/Azure SDK producing findings.
Auto-remediate low-risk findings safely.

topics.title: Benchmarks
details: CIS controls are concrete checks (e.g. 'Ensure MFA is enabled for the root user'); each has an audit and remediation procedure.

topics.title: Scanner design
details: Check registry, read-only credentials, parallel region scans, findings with severity, resource ID and fix; output JSON/SARIF.

topics.title: Auto-remediation
details: Only for low-risk, reversible fixes (block public S3 access), with dry-run, exemption tags and logging.

reading.locator: CIS Benchmarks page: download the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark (free registration) and read the Identity and Access Management and Logging sections.

assignment.title: Mini CSPM
instructions: Implement 20 CIS checks for AWS (and 5 for Azure) in Python with read-only credentials.
Test against an intentionally misconfigured sandbox built with Terraform.
Add one Lambda auto-remediation with dry-run and an exemption tag.
deliverables: Scanner code, test environment and results.
acceptanceCriteria: Every planted misconfiguration is found.
Remediation respects exemptions.

questions.prompt: Why should a posture scanner use read-only credentials?
questions.answer: Scanning should never be able to change resources.
questions.explanation: Least privilege for the tool itself.

questions.prompt: Which fixes are safe to automate?
questions.answer: Low-risk, reversible ones such as blocking public bucket access.

reviewPrompts: Pick three CIS controls you consider most important.
How do exemption tags work?

requirements: AWS emulator on your laptop: Floci (`docker run -p 4566:4566 floci/floci`, no account) or LocalStack (free non-commercial account and auth token), both on http://localhost:4566
Build the intentionally misconfigured environment with Terraform on the emulator and point your boto3 scanner at `endpoint_url='http://localhost:4566'`.
Compare your check list with Prowler's CIS checks (free, open source); running Prowler itself is best done later on a real Free plan account.
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: The emulator runs the same API calls, CLI commands and Terraform as AWS, so the skills transfer. It does not prove real AWS performance, real IAM enforcement in every service, real networking or real billing. Say 'built and tested against an AWS emulator' unless you also ran the optional real-cloud step.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: Optional real-cloud step: an AWS account on the Free plan (up to $200 credits for 6 months; no charges unless you upgrade to the paid plan). Never click 'upgrade', set a $1 budget alert anyway, and delete everything after the session. Use read-only credentials for the scanner on real AWS.

lessons.title: Policy as code: scanning Terraform and enforcing guardrails
objectives: Scan Terraform with Checkov/tfsec in CI.
Write custom policies for your organisation's rules.
Map technical controls to frameworks (CIS, ISO 27001, SOC 2) at a high level.

topics.title: Shift left
details: Catch misconfigurations in pull requests before they reach the cloud; fail on high-severity issues.

topics.title: Custom policies
details: Encode your rules ('all buckets must have tags owner and data_class') in Checkov custom checks or OPA/Rego.

topics.title: Compliance
details: Frameworks describe what to achieve; your controls and evidence show how. Automate evidence collection where possible.

reading.locator: Checkov docs: 'Quick start', 'CLI command reference' and 'Custom policies' (Python and YAML).

assignment.title: Guardrails in CI
instructions: Add Checkov to the CI of a Terraform repository; fix all high findings.
Write two custom policies for your own rules and test them with failing examples.
Map five of your controls to CIS and ISO 27001 categories in a table.
deliverables: CI workflow, custom policies and mapping table.
acceptanceCriteria: Custom policies fail on bad examples and pass on good ones.

questions.prompt: What does shift-left mean for cloud security?
questions.answer: Finding misconfigurations in code review/CI before deployment.
questions.explanation: Cheaper and safer than fixing in production.

questions.prompt: Framework vs control?
questions.answer: A framework states objectives; controls are the concrete measures that meet them.

reviewPrompts: Write a custom policy idea for tagging.
How would you automate compliance evidence?

requirements: Checkov, tfsec/Trivy config and OPA/Conftest (all free) on your laptop and in GitHub Actions.
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: Everything in this lab already runs for ₹0 on your laptop or in a free browser lab.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: None needed.

modules.title: 11. Security certifications and portfolio
modules.description: Plan certifications that open doors (Security+, AZ-500, AWS Security Specialty) and present your lab work as a portfolio.

lessons.title: Certification plan and a security portfolio
objectives: Choose a certification order based on your Azure background.
Build a study schedule with practice exams.
Present lab projects as a portfolio recruiters can verify.

topics.title: Certifications
details: Security+ proves broad fundamentals; AZ-500 builds on your Azure certifications; AWS Certified Security - Specialty for AWS roles.

topics.title: Study method
details: Exam objectives as a checklist, video course, hands-on labs for each objective, timed practice exams, review every wrong answer.

topics.title: Portfolio
details: GitHub repos with READMEs for your scanner, signed pipeline and detection lab; write-ups of what you found and fixed.

video.locator: Use as the Security+ primary course; follow it in order alongside the exam objectives.

reading.locator: AZ-500 certification page: the 'Skills measured' outline and the linked free training paths.

assignment.title: Twelve-week plan
instructions: Write a 12-week study plan for your first security certification with weekly objectives and labs.
Map each portfolio project to exam objectives and job description keywords.
Polish READMEs for your three security projects.
deliverables: Study plan and updated READMEs.
acceptanceCriteria: Each week has measurable goals and a lab.

questions.prompt: Why might AZ-500 suit you well?
questions.answer: It builds on your existing Azure knowledge and certifications.
questions.explanation: Faster path to a credible security credential.

questions.prompt: What makes a security portfolio credible?
questions.answer: Reproducible labs with clear write-ups of findings and fixes.

reviewPrompts: Which certification first and why?
How will you schedule practice exams?

requirements: Professor Messer's free Security+ videos, Microsoft Learn's free AZ-500 modules and AWS Skill Builder's free courses.
practiceEnvironment.evidenceBoundary: Study is free; exams are paid. Book only when practice scores are consistently strong.
practiceEnvironment.unavailableAction: Look for official exam discounts and vouchers (for example Microsoft Learn challenges) before paying full price.

limitations: Skill-builder lessons are beginner-first: each one assumes you have not used the tool before and explains the vocabulary before the practice.
Readings are official documentation or free books, linked rather than copied. Check the current version when you open a link; tools change.
Use your own machine, free tiers and synthetic or public data. Never use employer code, client data or credentials in exercises.
Defensive and authorised only: test, scan and simulate attacks only in accounts, clusters and lab machines you own.

Every lab has a ₹0 path (local tools, an AWS emulator, kind, Keycloak, Wazuh or GitHub Actions) shown under 'Practise for ₹0'. Real AWS or Azure steps are optional and use only plans that cannot charge you unless you upgrade.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Explain core security concepts, cryptography and identity, and write least-privilege policies.
stageOutcomes.evidence: Threat model, policy tests and notes that a reviewer could check.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Secure AWS and Azure accounts and find common application vulnerabilities.
stageOutcomes.evidence: Hardened sandbox accounts with logging and detections, plus fixed lab vulnerabilities.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Secure the software supply chain and Kubernetes, and engineer detections.
stageOutcomes.evidence: A signed-image pipeline with admission control and validated Sigma rules.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Respond to incidents, automate posture management and prepare for certifications.
stageOutcomes.evidence: Incident playbooks, a posture scanner and a certification study plan.
